title: How to create a custom client portal with AI safely
summary: Learn how to build a custom client portal with AI. Set up client logins, secure permissions and workflows with Noloco. 7 easy steps.
body_markdown:
Your clients want to know what’s happening with their projects. They want to upload documents, approve work, check deadlines and get answers without having to email your team every time.


Your team wants the same thing: fewer status-update emails, fewer files scattered across folders, and less time spent chasing clients for information.


A client portal can solve these problems. But building one has traditionally meant hiring a developer, wrestling with a rigid template or spending weeks trying to connect tools that weren’t designed for your business.


AI changes that.


With an AI portal builder like Noloco, you can upload your existing business data, describe the client portal you want in plain English, and let AI help build it. Need to change the dashboard, add an approval button or adjust who can access certain information? Just ask.


You don’t need to write code. And you don’t have to settle for a generic portal that forces your business to work differently.


In this guide, we’ll walk through how to build a custom client portal with AI, including how to set up permissions, create useful workflows and give your clients a better way to work with your team.


## What is a client portal?


A client portal is a private online space where your clients can interact with your business.


Instead of relying on email threads, shared spreadsheets and scattered documents, clients log in to one place to find the information and tools they need.


Depending on your business, your client portal might let clients:


- Check the progress of their projects.
- View upcoming deadlines and outstanding tasks.
- Upload files and share documents.
- Submit new requests.
- Review and approve completed work.
- Contact their account manager.
- Receive notifications when something needs their attention.


Your internal team can use the same system to manage projects, assign tasks, update statuses and respond to client requests.


The result? Your team and your clients work from the same information, without everyone needing access to everything.


The important part is that your portal should fit how your business works. A consultancy managing client projects needs something different from a solar company coordinating installations or a finance team collecting documents for monthly reporting.


That’s why building a custom client portal can be more useful than trying to squeeze your process into a one-size-fits-all template.


## Why build your client portal with AI?


Traditional portal projects often involve a long list of decisions: which pages to create, how to display data, what actions users need, and how to manage access.


With AI, you can describe the outcome you want instead of building everything from scratch.


For example, you could tell an AI portal builder:


> “Create a client portal where customers can see their active projects, check deadlines, upload documents and approve completed work. Show overdue projects at the top of the dashboard, and include a button to contact their account manager.”


Rather than manually building every element, you can use that description as the starting point for your portal.


But building a portal is only part of the job. If real clients will use it, you also need to control what they can see and do, and make sure the portal supports your actual workflow.


That’s where an AI portal builder with real permissions matters.


With Noloco, you use[Nola](https://noloco.io/product/nola) in Canvas to build and refine your portal through conversation. You can describe what you need, ask for changes and use AI to help configure permissions, all without writing code.


Let’s see how that works in practice.


## Step 1: Prepare your business data


Before building your portal, gather the information you want it to use.


You don’t need to design every screen first. Start by thinking about what your clients need to know and what your team needs to manage behind the scenes.


For a project-based business, that might include:


- **Clients:** Names, contact details and account managers.
- **Projects:** Project names, descriptions, deadlines and current status.
- **Tasks:** Work to complete, assigned team members, due dates and progress.
- **Files:** Documents, deliverables and other project-related files.
- **Internal team:** Team members, responsibilities and roles.


Upload your data to Noloco to give Nola the information it needs to help build your portal.


If you’re already managing your business in spreadsheets or another supported data source, you may be able to use that existing data rather than starting again.


The goal is to create a useful foundation for your portal, not to rebuild your entire business before you can get started.


**A practical tip:** Start with one real workflow. If your biggest problem is clients constantly asking for project updates, begin with client records, projects, tasks and deadlines. You can expand the portal later.


## Step 2: Describe the client portal you want


Now comes the part where AI makes building a portal much more approachable.


Open Nola in Canvas and describe the portal you want to create. Be as specific as possible about what clients should see, what they should be able to do, and how you want information presented.


You don’t need technical terminology. Think about how you’d explain the portal to a colleague.


For example, instead of asking for “a client dashboard”, explain what a useful dashboard means for your business.


### Example prompt: Build a client project portal


Copy and adapt this prompt for your own business:


> Build a client portal for our project-based business using the data I’ve uploaded.
>
>
> Each client should have a dashboard where they can:
>
>
> - See their active projects and current project status.
> - View upcoming deadlines and outstanding tasks.
> - See overdue projects at the top of the dashboard.
> - Access relevant project files and deliverables.
> - Upload documents requested by our team.
> - Approve completed work using a clear action button.
> - Contact their account manager directly.
>
>
> Make the dashboard easy to understand, with the most important information at the top. Use clear status labels so clients can see what needs their attention.
>
>
> Our internal team needs a separate view where they can manage all projects, update tasks and deadlines, and see which clients are waiting for a response.
>
>
> Help me set up the permissions so each client can access only their own information, while internal team members can access the information they need for their roles.


This gives Nola a clear picture of what you’re trying to achieve.


You can then review what it builds and ask for adjustments. You don’t have to get every detail right in your first prompt.


## Step 3: Refine the dashboard with simple instructions


A useful client portal isn’t just a place to store information. It should help people understand what needs their attention and what to do next.


Once Nola has created the initial portal, look at it from your client’s perspective.


Can they find their current projects quickly? Is it obvious which tasks are overdue? Can they approve work without sending an email?


If something isn’t quite right, tell Nola what to change. Here are a few examples:


**To make important information easier to find:**


> “Show overdue projects first, followed by projects with deadlines in the next seven days.”


**To make project status clearer:**


> “Add a clear status indicator to each project so clients can distinguish between work in progress, work waiting for their input and completed work.”


**To help clients find what they need:**


> “Add a section to the dashboard showing documents we’ve requested from each client and whether they’ve been uploaded.”


**To make the next action obvious:**


> “Add an approval button to completed deliverables so clients can review and approve work directly from the portal.”


**To make contacting your team easier:**


> “Add a button that lets clients contact their assigned account manager from their project page.”


These are ordinary business instructions, not coding tasks.


You can keep refining the portal as you see what works. Ask Nola to update the dashboard, change how information is displayed or adjust the layout to make common tasks easier.


The aim is to give clients a portal that helps them get things done, rather than another system they have to learn.


## Step 4: Set up permissions with AI


This is one of the most important steps when building a client portal.


Your clients should be able to access their own projects, documents and tasks. They shouldn’t be able to browse another client’s information or see internal notes intended for your team.


At the same time, your internal team may need access to multiple clients, depending on their responsibilities.


Getting these rules right is essential when your portal contains real business information.


With Noloco, you can use AI to help set up[permissions](https://noloco.io/product/permissions) , too. Rather than having to work out every rule through manual configuration, you can describe who should see what and what they’re allowed to do.


### Example prompts for client portal permissions


**Separate each client’s information:**


> “Make sure each client can only see their own projects, tasks and files. They must not be able to access information belonging to other clients.”


**Control what clients can change:**


> “Allow clients to view project progress, upload requested documents and approve completed deliverables, but don’t let them edit internal task assignments or deadlines.”


**Give account managers the access they need:**


> “Let each account manager access the projects and client information assigned to them. Other account managers’ client records should remain restricted.”


**Keep internal notes private:**


> “Keep internal project notes and team discussions hidden from clients, while allowing clients to see project updates intended for them.”


These instructions describe the outcome you need. Nola can help configure the corresponding permissions through AI.


You can also adjust the rules as your business changes. If you introduce a new role or change what clients are allowed to do, describe the new requirements to Nola.


### Don’t skip the access checks


AI makes setting up permissions easier, but you should still verify that the resulting rules behave as intended before inviting clients.


Test the portal with representative user accounts:


- Can one client see only the information intended for them?
- Can they access their own files and complete the actions available to them?
- Are internal notes and restricted information hidden from clients?
- Can an account manager access the clients and projects assigned to them?
- Are users prevented from accessing information outside their permissions?


Check the actual access rules and the resulting behavior, not just what the dashboard looks like.


A good-looking portal is not necessarily a properly restricted portal. The goal is to combine AI-assisted building with access controls that match the way your business operates.


## Step 5: Create workflows and notifications


A client portal becomes much more useful when it helps move work forward.


Think about the situations that currently trigger emails, reminders and follow-ups from your team. Many of these can become part of your portal[workflow](https://noloco.io/product/workflows) .


For example, you might want a notification when a client submits a request, an approval is waiting, or a deadline is approaching.


You can describe the workflow you want to Nola and ask it to help configure the changes.


**Notify your team when a client submits a request:**


> “Set up a workflow so that when a client submits a new project request, our internal team is notified and the request is available for review.”


**Make approvals easier:**


> “Set up the client approval process so that clients can approve completed deliverables from the portal. Make the approval status visible to our team so they know which items are still waiting for a response.”


**Highlight overdue work:**


> “Highlight overdue tasks and projects on the internal dashboard so our team can see what needs attention first.”


**Keep clients informed:**


> “Notify the relevant client when their project status changes or a new deliverable is ready for review.”


These are starting prompts. The exact workflow should reflect your business rules: who receives the notification, what triggers it and what should happen next.


The benefit is that you can describe how you want work to move through your business, then use AI to help shape the portal around that process.


## Step 6: Make the portal feel like your business


Your clients shouldn’t feel as though they’re logging into a generic tool that happens to contain their information.


Your portal is part of the experience you provide, so it should feel consistent with the way you work with clients.


Review the portal’s branding, navigation, labels and page layouts. You might ask Nola to:


- “Use our company branding throughout the portal.”
- “Rename ‘Tasks’ to ‘Action items’ so the wording matches how we communicate with clients.”
- “Make the project overview the first page clients see after logging in.”
- “Simplify the navigation so clients can find projects, documents and approvals easily.”


Small changes like these can make the portal feel more natural to use.


The same principle applies to the information you show. Use labels your clients understand, rather than internal terminology that only makes sense to your team.


For example, “Waiting for your approval” is more useful to a client than an internal status code they have to ask you to explain.


## Step 7: Test the portal before inviting clients


Before you launch, take time to check that the portal works for the people who will use it.


Don’t just test it as an administrator. Log in using representative client and internal team accounts, and walk through the tasks each person needs to complete.


Use this checklist as a starting point:


- Clients can log in and find their own projects.
- Each client sees only the information they’re permitted to access.
- Internal notes and restricted information aren’t visible to clients.
- Clients can upload the documents they need to share.
- Approval buttons perform the intended action.
- Project statuses and deadlines display correctly.
- Notifications go to the intended people.
- Internal team members can access the information needed for their roles.
- The portal is easy to navigate without help from your team.


If something needs changing, you can ask Nola to adjust the portal and test the result again.


This is particularly important when you change permissions or workflows. A small change can affect more than one part of your portal, so verify the behavior that matters before rolling it out to clients.


Once you’re happy with the result, invite your clients and give them a clear explanation of how to use the portal.


## What happens when your business changes?


Your client portal shouldn’t become another system you outgrow.


As your business grows, you might introduce new services, change approval processes, add account managers or give clients access to additional information.


With a traditional custom-built application, those changes can require developer time and additional maintenance.


With Noloco, you can use Nola to keep adapting your portal. Describe the new requirement, ask for the change and refine the result. For example:


> “We’re introducing a new service. Add a section where clients can submit requests for it, including the information our team needs to review each request.”


Or:


> “We’ve added a new account manager. Update the relevant access rules so they can manage their assigned clients without accessing restricted records.”


Your portal can evolve alongside your business instead of forcing you to start again whenever your process changes.


And you aren’t limited to a client-facing portal. You can expand the same system to support internal workflows, project delivery, team coordination and other parts of your operation as your needs grow.
